subject: dwarfRifleman
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: dwarf rifleman with braided beard and blunderbuss.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a dwarf rifleman model's proportions and skeleton structure, aiming for a stocky build around 1.3-1.4 meters tall with hips positioned as the root joint.

I'm settling on a color palette that leans into a Warcraft-inspired Ironforge dwarf look—ruddy skin, ginger beard, blue and brass armor accents, and a steel dome helmet with brass trim and forehead goggles—while figuring out how to rig the beard braids, arms, legs, and blunderbuss attachment to a hand bone.

Defining hip and spine joints...

Still placing head joints...

Now I'm working out the torso loft, building station cross-sections along the hip-to-spine path and figuring out how the bone chain should drive the loft shape and width/depth parameters at each station.

I'm reconsidering the bone hierarchy for the torso sweep — having hips and spine joints at the same position creates a zero-length bone, so I'm adjusting by offsetting the spine joint slightly above hips, or possibly dropping hips entirely and using just the spine chain as the sweep path.

Placing hips and spine joints at identical coordinates would create a zero-length bone, so I need an offset instead. For the legs, I'm computing hip socket positions and foot targets for short dwarf proportions, checking that thigh plus shin length comfortably reaches the ankle with a slight bend, and setting the knee to bend forward using the limb function.

For the leg chain, I'm naming the three joints hip, knee, and ankle per side, parenting to the hips, and varying the sweep radius along the chain to make the thighs bulkier and the shins narrower with boots. I've decided to draw boots as separate parts rather than folding them into the sweep, combining a foot box with a shaft cylinder for each leg.

Still working out the bone binding...

For the leg chain I'll reference joints as hip, knee, and ankle, with the tip being the ankle. For the foot I'm shaping the toe cap and a darker sole slab beneath a boot box, sizing the foot roughly 0.15 wide and 0.1 tall centered low to the ground.

Now for the sole piece I'm sizing it as a thin box sitting at the lowest point so the boots touch down at y=0. For arms, I'm positioning shoulders with large pauldrons and posing them holding a blunderbuss forward, right hand gripping behind the trigger and left hand supporting the barrel.

I'm reconsidering a neutral A-pose instead — left arm relaxed outward with open fingers, right arm angled out gripping the blunderbuss so it rests forward-up at the side, keeping the pose readable rather than a strict two-handed firing stance.

For hands, I'm weighing simplified geometry: a palm box with finger chains (two joints each) for the open left hand, roughly ten joints total, while the right hand's fingers curl around the grip. I need to keep the total joint count under the 160 limit once everything is tallied.

I'm sketching a general makeHand helper that takes side, wrist position/joint, and curl state, defining each finger by a base offset, direction, and a short polyline path (base, mid, tip) to approximate the curled or open pose.

I'll give each hand four fingers plus a thumb, each as a two-joint chain swept with tapering radii for a bending capsule look, totaling twenty joints across both hands. Now I'm positioning the left arm in an A-pose, setting shoulder and elbow coordinates and upper arm/forearm lengths to figure out the natural tilt angle.

Continuing on, I'm calculating the elbow and wrist positions by normalizing the arm direction vectors and extending them by segment length, then placing the hand slightly beyond the wrist to sit at hip level. I'll build the arm as a chain from shoulder through elbow to wrist, parented to the chest, with named joints for each point and a tangent-aligned tip for the wrist.

For mirroring left and right limbs, I'm looping over a sign variable so +X corresponds to the left side, appending "L"/"R" suffixes to joint names, and tapering the tube radius smoothly from shoulder to wrist. I'm now working out the right arm's bent-forward pose for the gun-holding hand, computing shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates so the forearm angles horizontally toward a grip position at hip level.

I'm figuring out how to model the gun itself relative to the hand position, defining a local axis system along the gun's forward direction so I can place cylindrical parts (barrel, grip, stock) using helper coordinates built from the gun's forward, up, and lateral vectors rather than absolute world coordinates.

For the barrel's muzzle flare, I could sweep along the breech-to-muzzle line with a radius function that grows into a bell shape at the end, explicitly specifying the bone rather than relying on tuple-to-joint inference.

For the radius profile along the sweep, I'm thinking a slow taper from 0.028 to 0.034 for most of the length, then a smooth flare out to 0.075 near the muzzle. For a low-poly faceted look, I'd use 8 sides with smooth shading off, and add extra rings wherever the radius changes rapidly. For the muzzle bell specifically, lathing an outline profile around the barrel's axis direction might work better than sweeping.

Writing lathe outline points...

Defining the stock as a tapered frustum box from breech to butt, setting up its angled position and lateral/vertical dimensions with sloped width and height values.

Checking that the butt placement clears the body—positioned outside the hip radius near the torso, with a slight unavoidable overlap near the elbow that seems acceptable. Now I'm moving on to sketching the receiver and lock as a small brass box, with details for the hammer and trigger guard to follow.

I'm working out the pistol grip geometry—a small wood box angled below the receiver along the barrel axis—and positioning the hand to wrap around it, placing the wrist and palm center relative to the grip location.

Now I'm figuring out the hand mechanics: a right hand gripping a vertical pistol grip has the palm against one side with fingers curling forward across the grip and tips emerging on the other side, while the thumb wraps back on the palm side—so I'm laying out finger capsules running laterally at staggered heights to mimic that curl.

For simplicity I'm defining each finger as a short polyline of base/mid/tip points with a two-joint chain, using a shared helper for both hands, then setting up the left hand's wrist position and forearm direction so its fingers extend outward in an open posture along that same axis.

Working out finger and thumb placement with splay and curl, then defining the palm as a box oriented along the hand's forward, width, and normal axes...

Actually, I realize constructing an explicit orientation is getting overcomplicated — I should just scope this down and hand-place things more simply rather than building a full basis-aligned part system.

I'll mirror left/right sides using a sign variable, and work out proportions for a stocky dwarf: short legs, solid torso, a larger head with a beard, all sized so the helmet tops out around 1.5m total height. Now I'm building the skull as a sphere primitive to anchor the head geometry.

Instead of relying on uncertain scale-array support in the part function, I'll scale the geometry itself via BufferGeometry.scale before creating the part—safer and more predictable. I'm defining a small ellipsoid helper that returns a scaled sphere geometry, and using flat shading on most parts for a faceted, low-poly look.

Now I'm working out the facial features: a bulbous nose sphere with slightly reddish skin tone, rosy cheek spheres, a heavy brow ridge above the eyes, and eyes built from layered spheres—a white sclera, a smaller blue iris pushed forward, and a tiny dark pupil—positioned symmetrically under the brow.

I'm computing the head skull geometry as an ellipsoid centered around y=1.24, then calculating exact surface depths to figure out where the eye socket sits relative to the skull curvature, and layering the eye sphere, iris, and pupil at increasing z-depths so they protrude naturally from the face surface.

Now I'm working out the nose placement — positioning it on the same skull surface calculation and sizing a fairly prominent ellipsoid for it, then considering whether nostrils need tiny dark spheres or can be skipped for simplicity.

For the beard, dwarves need something massive, so I'm planning a tapering sweep running from the jaw down to the chest, widening out near the bottom to cover a good portion of the torso, and thinking through breaking it into a few separate elements rather than one single sweep.

I'll cover the lower jaw with an ellipsoid base so the mouth hides beneath mustache and beard, leaving just eyes, brows, nose, and curled mustache sweeps visible. I'm giving the beard texture with a grain function that mixes two beard colors along the vertical axis for a strand-like look, and adding a couple of hanging braids built as jointed chains for extra dwarf flair.

Each braid path drops from near the chin down past the chest, and I'm populating it with alternating ellipsoid links using the chain's `along` helper so each segment inherits orientation from its point on the path—stretching them along the tangent direction and alternating slight rotations to get a twisted-braid effect.

Since rotation would override the frame's orientation, I'm pre-rotating the link geometry itself (alternating ±35° about Z based on index) before placing it with `b.part`, so the frame orientation still drives the overall sweep while the geometry carries the zigzag twist. I'm also planning to cap the braid ends with a small brass bead or ring.

For the beard itself, I'm imagining a tapered wedge mass of ginger hair reaching down to chest height, splitting at its base into three braids (a long central one and two side ones) that splay outward and terminate in brass rings, echoing the classic dwarven braided-beard look.

I should attach the beard to the head rigidly rather than the jaw, since jaw rotation would otherwise swing the whole beard mass unnaturally. The jaw itself probably needs its own skin-colored mesh with a lower lip and teeth, since the mouth is hidden behind the mustache and beard.

Setting jaw bone length around 0.16, positioned to aim toward the chin area. I'll skip visible teeth and just add a small dark mouth-cavity ellipsoid hidden beneath the mustache, since the closed mouth is mostly obscured anyway—only the jaw geometry really matters for the silhouette.

For the helmet, I'm designing a lathed steel dome shape with a brim band at the base, plus a brass spike on top; I'll skip a nose guard since it would hide the face, but add steel cheek plates on the sides.

I'm also adding goggles to the front with brass torus rings and blue-tinted lens spheres on a leather strap, giving that dwarven engineer look, and considering a small red-blue feather plume via a swept curve. Now I'm working out the precise helmet geometry—placing the head center, setting the top of the skull, and sizing the base ring radius to properly fit the helmet lathe profile onto the head.

Checking the helmet dome dimensions against the brow and eye placement to make sure the brim clears the forehead correctly, then tallying up total figure height including the helmet spike to see if it lands close to the target 1.5m dwarf scale.

Now I'm placing the small pointed ears tucked under cheek plates, and working out the ginger sideburns as ellipsoids sweeping down into the beard mass, plus curling mustache strands extending from under the nose outward.

I'm sketching bushy ginger eyebrow sweeps over each eye, then adding a short thick neck sweep connecting the chest to the head base, before moving on to the torso armor's blue tabard details.

Now I'm figuring out the torso layering: a blue cloth tunic beneath, then a leather bandolier harness crossing diagonally from shoulder to hip with attached pouches.

I need the decal to use alpha transparency so only the emblem shape shows against the metal. For the breastplate, I'm sweeping a separate path with a slightly larger radius than the torso at chest height, to sit just outside the torso surface without z-fighting.

Reusing the same torso path and radius function for the cuirass sweep, offset outward with flat caps so it wraps the whole chest and back as a steel plate, leaving the tunic visible below at the belly with a belt, and maybe a brass collar band at the top.

Defining radius profile...

I'm placing the shoulder pauldrons as steel half-domes with brass trim at the arm origins, sized relative to the chest width.

I'm deciding the pauldron should be rigid to the shoulder joint so it rotates with the arm, then working out the joint hierarchy -- naming spine and chest joints, with chest parenting the arms and neck.

Now I'm figuring out the hip joint's parent and sketching a belt around the waist by taking a loop from the torso surface at a fixed height.

For the buckle box, I'm making it flat with thickness along the normal so it sits embedded into the tunic, but I need to nudge it outward slightly so it doesn't sink into the belt itself.

I'm also checking that the belt loop placement at y=0.62 stays within the torso surface range rather than the cuirass or pauldron regions, and considering whether a lathe ring might be simpler than the surface API for the belt given the torso's elliptical cross-section.

For the bandolier, I'm draping a closed diagonal strap over the chest—running from the right shoulder down to the left hip and around the back—using catmull points, but need to decide whether it drapes onto the torso surface or the cuirass surface for the upper chest region, since the strap crosses both.

Since the rough path points sit outside the body at a larger radius, the nearest-surface calculation should naturally snap to whichever outer surface is closest, so I'm combining torso and cuirass into one surface set and letting nearest-point resolve it. Plotting the loop points...

Still placing cartridge shells...

Simplify to spheres for brass studs, then add a curved powder horn at the left hip using a swept tapered tube with a brass cap, plus a leather satchel or backpack with bedroll at the back.

I'm also designing a tabard with a shaped front flap panel extruded below the belt, oriented so its outline runs along the world X axis with a pointed bottom edge.

Settling on z=0.2 for the tabard with a gold trim stripe painted along the lower border, plus a small emblem decal. I'll skip the tassets and loincloth for now, and add steel bracer cuffs as a wider-radius sweep on the forearm segment of the arm chain.

For the arms, I'm splitting the sleeve into a blue tunic portion on the upper arm and bare skin on the forearm, using color bands along the sweep where the boundary falls around 0.52 of the chain length—matching the shoulder-to-elbow joint—then adding a cuff ring at that transition point.

Moving to hands, I'm giving both gloves a dark leather tone rather than bare skin, keeping them consistent since the bracers already cover the wrist transition. For legs, I'm deciding on dark brown trousers with leather boots in a near-black brown, finished with steel toe caps and brass buckle details at the knee.

Now I'm positioning small leather-and-steel knee pad discs using a rotated cylinder placed just forward of the knee joint, computing the offset from the limb's knee position so it sits naturally when the leg bends. I'm also planning tiny brass buckles and a folded cuff ring for the boot shaft.

I'm figuring out the boot shaft geometry as a cylinder spanning from ankle to mid-shin, matching its radius to the ankle width while accounting for the slight forward tilt of the shin bone so it still reads correctly against the angled leg.

I'll settle on using the ankle joint explicitly, with the shaft running from the ankle position to 60% toward the knee, keeping things simple for performance. Now I'm thinking through the Warcraft-style palette—Ironforge blue and gold, warm skin tones, red-orange hair, steel armor grays—while keeping the shared flat color count under the 64-color limit.

For the overall pitch I want that chunky Blizzard look: oversized pauldrons, exaggerated hands and boots, an oversize gun, all leaning into that stylized proportion.

Now I'm structuring the builder calls—setting up the dwarf's root joint at the hips with a spine role, then starting the spine chain.

Still writing chain and joint setup...

I'm using a single-joint neck chain with thin radius, keeping caps rounded and hidden inside the torso and head. For the torso bone path, I'm confirming it runs through tail, hips, spine, and head joints, then thinking about how to color the tunic—possibly with stripes or a gradient rather than flat blue.

Now I'm deciding on a flat blue tunic with subtle mottling for cloth texture, using the builder's paint options like mottle, stripes, grain, and gradient. I'm setting up the cuirass sweep along the same path with matching from/to radius values, widening the pelvis area, and defining a catmull spline for the torso path with control points to compute arc length and t-values for positioning.

I'm working out the torso's radial profile stops to shape the taper from hips to shoulders, then checking whether round caps at the top would extend too far upward into the chin/jaw area versus using flat caps to keep the neck and shoulder line properly placed.

Rather than fight that overlap, I'll switch to a flat-capped torso end at y=1.0 with a wider radius, then add a steel gorget collar to visually hide the neck join. So the torso caps become round at the start and flat at the end, and I'll move on to building the cuirass next.

Still defining cuirass shape and texture...

For surface attachments I'm checking how `skin.loop` orients on world-up for the cuirass sweep, then placing an emblem decal near the chest surface with a forward-facing direction. I'm sketching the emblem as a simple gold ring icon with crossed hammers on a transparent background, Ironforge-style.

Still writing anvil shape coordinates...

Adding a small gem accent, then moving to spiked pauldrons with layered plates and brass rivets, positioning a cone spike outward from the shoulder joint with proper axis orientation for left vs right sides.

Now I'm shaping the helmet with a lathed dome profile and faceted rim, then adding a brass band ring around its base, checking that the ring radius slightly overlaps the dome's curvature near the bottom.

For the crest, I'm extruding a fin-shaped outline along the front-to-back axis, positioning it above the dome so its base sits just within the dome's curved surface at that height, making sure the fin's width stays within the dome's radial extent so it doesn't clip through.

Adjusting crest height so it peaks higher at center, bringing total height to about 1.51 plus the plume. Now I'm shaping a curved red feather plume sweeping back from the crest using a bezier path with tapering radius.

Adjusting plume curve to a lower peak, then adding the goggle strap band, brass lens rings tilted upward and forward, and tinted blue lens circles positioned on the helmet.

I'm now repositioning the goggles to sit properly on the forehead rest area, adding a small bridge rod, then shaping the cheek guard flaps as extruded side profiles with defined thickness.

I'm deciding to skip horns or wings for this helmet design, keeping it simpler. For ears, I'm placing small skin ellipsoids near the cheek flaps, letting the flap cover down to where the ear sits so I can skip detailing visible ears entirely.

For the beard, I'm picking a ginger color palette with highlights and a streaky grain pattern for texture, then shaping the beard mass as a spade-like sweep from the chin downward with varying width along its length.

Checking the beard against the torso, I realize it would overlap and hide the cuirass emblem decal on the chest, so I need to either shorten the beard or reposition the emblem to avoid the clash.

I'm reconsidering the beard shape entirely -- instead of a single central beard, I'll fork it into two side braids at roughly ±0.06 spacing, which matches typical dwarf styling and keeps the chest emblem visible since the braids won't cross the center.

Settling the emblem on the chest center and working out the braid paths with curved control points down the torso, checking the surface depth at each height so the braid radius clears the cuirass without clipping.

Setting up the braid chain parented to the jaw bone with named joints along its length, picking "tentacle" as the closest available role for a flexible hair braid, then building the visual geometry by placing link segments along the chain frames.

I'm being careful to generate a fresh geometry instance for each link rather than reusing one, since the SDK might mutate geometry in place during transforms—keeping the total part count comfortably under the limit.

Working out link dimensions so the capsules overlap slightly for a zigzag braided look, tapering the radius along the braid using a scale factor, and alternating colors between the two beard tones with a brass ring and tassel planned for the tie.

Still placing the brass ring and tip cone geometry...

Now I'm moving on to the hands. I'm computing wrist direction vectors from the arm chain to orient a palm box with appropriate dimensions, placing it slightly forward along the forearm direction, and planning leather glove coloring with a steel cuff accent.

For the fingers, I'm positioning four digits offset along the width axis, with the thumb at the front edge (anatomically correct for a left hand hanging palm-inward), and varying finger lengths so the middle one is longest.

Still writing finger joint chains...

Now I'm working out the right hand and gun grip positioning, placing the wrist joint from the right arm chain and computing the grip center offset forward and down from it.

I'm defining the gun's internal coordinate space—receiver box dimensions and the wooden grip position below it—so the hand center aligns with where fingers would wrap the grip.

I compute origin O by offsetting from the hand position along the gun and up vectors, then lay out the stock as a box stretching back from the receiver, and the barrel as a tube that tapers slightly before flaring into a bell shape near the muzzle, giving a total length of about 1.24m from butt to muzzle, which seems oversized.

I trim the barrel and bell lengths and recompute the muzzle position so the total length stays reasonable while keeping the pose angled correctly. I add a thin ramrod cylinder running under the barrel and brass ring bands spaced along the barrel's length using small hollow cylinder geometries.

Now I'm working out the hammer, trigger, and trigger guard geometry, trying a bezier sweep curve approach for the guard shape since a simple torus segment feels too fiddly.

Then I'm adding finishing details: a flared lathe-turned muzzle, a brass buttplate at the stock end, grain texture painted along the wood stock, and a small cone sight near the muzzle.

I'm double-checking box orientation conventions so that each part's lateral, length, and vertical dimensions align correctly with the gun's tilted axis, confirming the frustum box helper handles sideways and normal directions properly for the stock shape.

Now I'm setting up a coordinate helper function to position gun parts using gun axis, up vector, and lateral vectors, then working out where each finger wraps around the grip—placing them vertically stacked with spacing matched to typical finger diameter as they curl from the right side across the front to the left side.

Still working out finger coordinates...

Checking the palm center against the wrist position confirms the offset works nicely, with the palm sitting slightly forward of the wrist along a diagonal. Now I'm working out the thumb's path as it wraps from the palm up around the back of the grip toward the left side.

For the fingers, I'll parent each chain to the wrist joint using a shared helper function, since orientation within each chain doesn't matter much. The gun itself attaches rigidly to the wrist bone, and the right arm uses a simple polyline chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist—I'm now considering adding bracer armor as a sweep along that arm chain.

Working out bracer placement using the forearm's span range, interpolating the start and end points along that segment and tapering the radius from shoulder toward elbow with a sequence of decreasing values.

Checking that the fixed bracer radius clears the forearm's natural radius at both wrist and elbow, then moving on to legs — figuring out hip and thigh mount positions off the limb coordinates.

The torso's rounded bottom cap extends down near the pelvis enough to cover the crotch region without clipping the leg roots, so that geometry checks out. For the legs, I'm computing the distance from hip to foot target against the combined thigh and shin lengths to find how far forward the knee needs to bow, treating it as a triangle with the two limb segments as sides.

I'm figuring out the `limb` function's signature, taking root, target, lengths, and bend hints, and returning a point array that can feed directly into the chain builder as a polyline path. Now I'm assigning taper radii along the leg sweep, going from a thicker hip radius down to a narrower ankle, so the limb reads as naturally rounded through the knee bend.

Now I'm sketching the boot geometry: a steel toe cap as a flattened sphere up front, a dark sole box underneath, and a darker heel block at the back, sizing each piece so they overlap sensibly with the main foot box without poking through.

For the shin, I'm building a tapered rod from ankle up to roughly 62% toward the knee, with a flat-capped cylinder plus a cuff band folded over near the top for the boot shaft.

I'm adding a darker leather cuff band and a small brass buckle positioned as a flat vertical plate on the front of the shin, then planning the knee pads and a leather backpack box next.

For the backpack I'm placing a chest bone anchor and a tan bedroll cylinder lashed across the top, plus a hanging steel mug or pot and a darker flap with a brass buckle -- then considering whether to add a beer mug or dagger hanging from the belt.

Now I'm roughing out a tankard at the back-left hip with a small handle torus, then tallying up the overall part count across the figure -- torso, cuirass bands, rivets, bandolier studs, legs with boots, arms with bracers and spiked pauldrons, fingers, and a detailed head and helmet -- to get a sense of the total model complexity.

I'm deciding which SDK helpers to import, keeping the list minimal to avoid unused-import errors, and planning to use THREE.Vector3 directly for vector math instead of extra helper functions. Writing dwarf color palette and metadata...

Now I'm building the skeleton hierarchy — defining a hips joint and a spine chain built from a catmull curve, with chest derived from the second spine joint, thinking through how the hips bone connects to its spine and leg children.

Continuing the skeleton, I'm chaining a neck segment off the chest using a polyline, then attaching head and jaw joints with aim directions for proper orientation. Now I'm starting to define the torso shape itself using a catmull curve with width/depth stops along its path to build out the body silhouette...

Writing the torso profile function...

I'm sweeping the torso curve into a solid shape with elliptical cross-sections, parented to hips and spine, using a tunic-colored paint and mixed start/end cap styles -- and bumping the polygon sides up to 12 so the belly doesn't look too faceted.

Then I'm layering a cuirass over the lower portion of the torso by offsetting the radius slightly outward, flattening the caps, and adding color bands near the chest and shoulders to simulate gold trim over steel armor -- checking that the band placement lines up roughly with the neckline and arclength position.

For coloring the cuirass, I decide it's safer to use a paint function that checks the sweep position and returns gold near the edges and steel elsewhere, since paint functions can return nested paints, avoiding ambiguity with band color strings. Then I'm adding a skin-toned neck sweep and a steel gorget ring at the collar to visually mask the seam where the neck meets the torso, designing its outline to taper and curve around the join.

The lathe ring's radius mismatches the torso's elliptical top, so I drop that approach and instead plan a torus geometry for the collar: rotate it to lie flat, then scale it non-uniformly so its radii match the torso width and depth, giving a thick fur-lined collar placed just above the torso-neck seam in a cream color.

Now I'm setting up the shoulder/arm rig: for each side I'm defining shoulder, elbow, and wrist points, then checking that the upper-arm and forearm segment lengths come out roughly equal on both sides and fit naturally against the torso's curved silhouette at the elbow height.

I'm also sanity-checking that the stock/weapon mesh passes below and outside the elbow and hip geometry without clipping, then I'm building the arm chain structure with named bone segments parented to the chest.

Now I'm defining the sweep that generates the arm's tube mesh with tapering radii from shoulder to wrist, and setting up a color function that splits the texture into sleeve-colored and skin-colored bands based on position along the arm, adjusting the split point to roughly match the elbow joint.

For the pauldron and hand geometry, I'm planning to reuse the shoulder and wrist joints from the arm chain, then write a reusable helper function for building finger chains with their own polyline points, sweep radii, and colors.

Writing finger-building helper...

I'm verifying joint naming stays unique across fingers and thumb, then tallying up the total joint count across legs, arms, hands, braids, spine, neck, head, jaw and hips to make sure I stay under the 160 limit.

Computing wrist position for hand layout...

I'm working out the forward and up vectors for the palm orientation relative to the elbow-to-wrist direction, then placing the palm box with appropriate dimensions and orientation.

Now I'm computing finger placement, varying lengths per finger and offsetting them across the palm width, with each finger split into two segments (base to mid, mid to tip) along the hand's forward direction.

For the thumb, I'm positioning it separately with its own base, mid, and tip offsets using a mix of sideways, forward, and inward vectors so it angles naturally relative to the fingers.

I'm deciding to skip a glove cuff since the bracer already covers that area, and now I need to make sure the gun frame coordinates are defined before the arm loop runs, since the right hand's fingers reference the gun's position when gripping it.

I'm setting up a tilted gun direction and up vector, computing an origin point near the grip, and building a helper function G(u,v,w) that maps along-gun, up, and lateral offsets into world space -- checking that it correctly reproduces the grip center when plugged with the right offsets, and confirming the lateral sign convention puts the right hand on the correct side. Now I'm sketching out the right hand's palm box dimensions relative to this grip frame.

Positioning fingers along the grip...

Checking the vertical extents confirms the fingers fit within the grip's range nicely, with radii tapering from 0.016 to 0.012 across six sides. Now I'm moving on to positioning the thumb.

For the thumb I'm wrapping it around the back of the grip near u=-0.07, overlapping opposite the fingers as is typical for a grip, but I need to shift its vertical placement upward to v=+0.012 to avoid colliding with finger 0, keeping it near the receiver's lower edge instead.

Adjusting finger and grip offsets...

Still placing gun parts...

Modeling the stock with a tapered frustum shape and wood grain texture, then adding a buttplate box at the rear end.

Now I'm placing small brass medallion discs on both sides of the cheek area, using cylinder geometry pre-rotated so the axis aligns laterally once the overall direction orientation is applied.

For the barrel, I'm building it as a tapered rod from the chamber to muzzle using steel coloring and octagonal sides, then adding a brass lathe-turned bell shape at the muzzle end oriented along the barrel axis, followed by brass band cylinders placed along the barrel.

For the brow ridge, I'm sizing a small ellipsoid positioned just above the eyes so it casts a slight shadow over them, matching the head's curvature at that height. I'll give it a slightly darker skin tone, then start sketching ginger eyebrows as a curved path sweeping across the brow surface.

Writing tabard extrude shape...

Still working out coloring logic...

I'm also considering placing the emblem on the cuirass rather than the thin tabard slab, and verifying the tabard's thickness axis points forward correctly. Then I'm working through the torso radius and belt placement math to make sure the tabard and belt sit just above the body surface without clipping.

Checking that the tabard hangs freely past the belt down to the thighs with a plausible gap from the leg geometry, and considering adding a matching rear flap at the opposite z-position.

For the hip pouches, I'm casting rays sideways from the torso to find attachment points on both sides, then sticking leather boxes sized for the pouch shape with the normal axis aligned outward, plus a small brass button sphere on the flap.
